<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="Amire80" /></noinclude><section begin=par72 /><section begin=par72 />Klostermann after the LXX. In {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dn|chapter=8|verse=11}} the {{GHGterm|K<sup>e</sup>thîbh}} {{GHGheb|text=הדים}} is intended for a {{GHGterm|perfect Hiphʿîl}}. There is also a distinction in meaning between {{GHGheb|text=יָלִין|translate=to spend the night, to remain}}, and {{GHGheb|text=יַלִּין}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=16|verse=7}} {{GHGterm|Q<sup>e</sup>rê}} ({{GHGterm|K<sup>e</sup>thîbh}} {{GHGheb|text=תּלּוֹנוּ}}; conversely, verse 2 {{GHGterm|K<sup>e</sup>thîbh}} {{GHGheb|text=יַלִּ֫ינוּ}}, {{GHGterm|Q<sup>e</sup>rê}} {{GHGheb|text=יִלּ֫וֹנוּ}}), {{GHGterm|participle}} {{GHGheb|text=מַלִּין}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=16|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=14|verse=27}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Nu|chapter=17|verse=20|hidebook=1}}, ''to be stubborn, obstinate'': in the latter sense from the form {{GHGheb|text=יָלִין}} only {{GHGheb|text=וַיָּ֫לֶן}} is found, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=17|verse=3}}. Other examples are {{GHGterm|Niphʿal}} {{GHGheb|text=נִמּוֹל|translate=he was circumcised}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=17|verse=26}} f.; {{GHGterm|participle}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=34|verse=22|hidebook=1}} (from {{GHGheb|text=מוּל}}, not {{GHGheb|text=נָמַל}}); {{GHGheb|text=נֵעוֹר|translate=he is waked up}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zc|chapter=2|verse=17}} (see above, v); {{GHGterm|Hiphʿîl}} {{GHGheb|text=הִזִּיל֫וּהַ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=La|chapter=1|verse=8}}; {{GHGheb|text=יַלִּ֫יזוּ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=4|verse=21}}.

{{GHGmargin-letter|72|ff}}
Perhaps the same explanation applies to some forms of verbs ''first guttural'' with ''Dageš forte implicitum'', which others derive differently or would emend, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=וַתַּ֫חַשׁ}} for {{GHGheb|text=וַתָּ֫חַשׁ|translate=and she hastened}} (from {{GHGheb|text=חוּשׁ}}) {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=31|verse=5}}; {{GHGheb|text=וַיַּ֫עַט}} (another reading is {{GHGheb|text=וַיָּ֫עַט}}), {{GHGheb|text=וַתַּ֫עַט}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=15|verse=19}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=25|verse=14|hidebook=1}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=14|verse=32|hidebook=1}} {{GHGterm|Q<sup>e</sup>rê}}) from {{GHGheb|text=עוּט}} or {{GHGheb|text=עִיט|translate=to fly at anything}}. Both, as far as the form is concerned, would be correct ''apocopated imperfects'' from {{GHGheb|text=חָשָׁה}} and {{GHGheb|text=עָטָה}} ({{GHGheb|text=ל״ה}}), but these stems only occur with a wholly different meaning.

{{GHGmargin-letter|72|gg}}
10. Verbs with a consonantal {{GHGterm|Wāw}} for their second radical, are inflected throughout like the strong form, provided the first or third radical is not a weak letter, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=חָוַר}}, {{GHGterm|imperfect}} {{GHGheb|text=יֶֽחֱוַר|translate=to be white}}; {{GHGheb|text=גָּוַע}}, {{GHGterm|imperfect}} {{GHGheb|text=יִגְוַע|translate=to expire}}; {{GHGheb|text=רָוַח|translate=to be wide}}; {{GHGheb|text=צָוַח|translate=to cry}}; {{GHGterm|Piʿēl}} {{GHGheb|text=עִוֵּל}}, {{GHGterm|imperfect}} {{GHGheb|text=יְעַוֵּל|translate=to act wickedly}}; {{GHGheb|text=עִוֵּת|translate=to bend}}, {{GHGterm|Hithpaʿēl}} {{GHGheb|text=הִתְעַוֵּת|translate=to bend oneself}}; and this is especially the case with verbs which are at the same time {{GHGheb|text=ל״ה}}, e.g. {{GHGheb|text=צָוָה}}, {{GHGterm|Piʿēl}} {{GHGheb|text=צִוָּה|translate=to command}}, {{GHGheb|text=קִוָּה|translate=to wait}}, {{GHGheb|text=רָוָה|translate=to drink}}, {{GHGterm|Piʿēl}} {{GHGheb|text=רִוָּה}} (on {{GHGheb|text=אֲרַיָּ֫וֶךְ}} {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=16|verse=9}}, see {{GHGpar|75|dd}}) and {{GHGterm|Hiphʿîl}} {{GHGheb|text=הִרְוָה|translate=to give to drink}}, &c.<section end=par72 />

<section begin=par73 />{{GHGpar-heading|73|Verbs middle i (vulgo {{GHGheb|text=ע״י}}), ''e.g.'' {{GHGheb|text=בִּין}} to discern. Paradigm N}}

{{GHGmargin-letter|73|a}}
'''1.''' These verbs agree, as regards their structure, exactly with verbs {{GHGheb|text=ע״וּ}}, and in contrast to them may be termed {{GHGheb|text=ע״י}}, or more correctly, ''ʿayin-î'' verbs, from the characteristic vowel of the ''impf., imper.'', and ''infin. constr''. This distinction is justified in so far as it refers to a difference in the pronunciation of the {{GHGterm|imperfect}} and its kindred forms, the {{GHGterm|imperative}} and ''infin. constr.''—the {{GHGheb|text=ע״וּ}} verbs having ''û'' lengthened from original ''ŭ'' and {{GHGheb|text=ע״י}} having ''î'' lengthened from original ''ĭ''. In other respects verbs {{GHGheb|text=ע״י}} simply belong to the class of really monosyllabic stems, which, by a strengthening of their ''vocalic'' element, have been assimilated to the triliteral form<ref>That verbs {{GHGheb|text=ע״וּ}} and {{GHGheb|text=ע״י}} are developed from biliteral roots at a period before the differentiation of the Semitic languages is admitted even by Nöldeke ({{GHGcite|title=Beiträge zur sem. Sprachwiss.}}, Strassburg, 1904, p. 34 ff.), although he contests the view that {{GHGheb|text=בִּינֹ֫תִי}} and {{GHGheb|text=רִיב֫וֹתָ}} are to be referred to {{GHGterm|Hiphʿîl}} with the preformative dropped.</ref> ({{GHGpar|67|a}}). In the {{GHGterm|perfect Qal}} the monosyllabic stem, as in {{GHGheb|text=ע״וּ}}, has ''ā'' lengthened from ''ă'', thus: {{GHGheb|text=שָׁת}} ''he has set; infinitive'' {{GHGheb|text=שִׁית}}, {{GHGterm|infinitive absolute}} {{GHGheb|text=שׁוֹת}}, {{GHGterm|imperative}} {{GHGheb|text=שִׁית}}, {{GHGterm|imperfect}} {{GHGheb|text=יָשִׁית}}, {{GHGterm|jussive}} {{GHGheb|text=יָשֵׁת}} ({{GHGpar|48|g}}), {{GHGterm|imperfect consecutive}} {{GHGheb|text=וַיָ֫שֶׁת}}.—The {{GHGterm|perfect Qal}} of some verbs<section end=par73 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>
